title: Civil War Battlefields
summary: Start with the 35 states of 1863 shaded by side, predict where the fighting happened, then turn on the battlefields and the railroads to test the prediction. Students use the pop-ups and Measure to explain why so much of the war was fought in a few places.
subject: History
alsoFits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration
time: About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

image.alt: The map as it opens: the United States, with 35 states shaded in two blues and two oranges and the western territories left unshaded.

map.about: This map shows the United States in the middle of 1863, two years into the Civil War. Each of the 35 states is shaded by its side and by when it seceded, if it did. Two layers are off when the map opens: the land where Civil War battles were fought, and the railroads in operation by 1863. State pop-ups give the side and the secession date; battlefield pop-ups give the name, the state and the size of the area.

layers.name: Civil War battlefields
layers.shows: A dark shape for each area the National Park Service maps as a battlefield of the Civil War years. At the national view each one looks like a dot. Almost every pop-up gives the name, the state and the size of the area in acres (two unnamed areas in Oklahoma do not). Off when the map opens.
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Railroads in operation by 1863
layers.shows: Thin black lines for the railroads in operation by 1863. They draw once you zoom in to a region. The pop-up gives the railroad's name (some lines have none), the year it was in operation by and the state. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: Jeremy Atack, Historical Geographic Information Systems database of U.S. Railroads

layers.name: The states in the Civil War, 1863
layers.shows: The 35 states of mid-1863 in four groups: Union free state (dark blue), Union slave state or border state (light blue), seceded before Fort Sumter (dark orange) and seceded after Fort Sumter (light orange). The pop-up gives the side, the secession date and, for some states, a note.
layers.source: Ordinances of secession and acts of admission; state outlines from Natural Earth

knownIssues.note: The layer does not say who won a battle or when it was fought, so no question asks for either. The pop-up says so.
The pop-up gives the state as a two-letter code. One battlefield's code is mistyped (Yellow Bayou, Louisiana, shows L0) and two small areas have no name.

Seventeen of the 378 areas are outside the 35 shaded states: fifteen named battlefields in the territories and Washington, D.C., and two unnamed areas in Oklahoma. Some in the West were fights between United States troops and Native nations in the war years; Bear River, Idaho, and Sand Creek, Colorado, were massacres of Native people. Question 7 uses these dots; teacher notes say more.

A few dots in the West mark attacks by United States troops on Native villages, including the massacres at Sand Creek, Colorado, and Bear River, Idaho. The layer lists every area as a battlefield; for these places that word does not fit.
Railroads draw only from about the regional view inward, so they do not show at The United States in 1863 bookmark. Questions 5 and 6 use the two regional bookmarks.

knownIssues.where: The states in the Civil War, 1863
knownIssues.note: State outlines are today's, and the territories and Nevada (a state from 1864) are not shaded. The side shown is the one each state joined, not who held its land in 1863.

compellingQuestion.en: By 1863 the United States had split in two. Where was the Civil War fought, and why there?

questions.task: With only the states layer on, students read the legend, sort the states into its four groups and use pop-ups to find when the first and last states seceded.
frontOfClass: Open The United States in 1863 bookmark and the legend.
Ask: what do the two blues have in common, and the two oranges?
Click South Carolina, then Tennessee, and read the date in each pop-up.
Ask: which light blue states touch an orange state?

steps.en: Open The United States in 1863 bookmark and open the legend.
Count the states in the two orange groups: each state's name is printed on it. The two blue groups are larger: 19 dark blue and 5 light blue.
Click South Carolina and Tennessee and read the date each seceded.

ask.en: (a) How many states seceded before Fort Sumter, and how many after? (b) Which side is blue and which is orange? (c) When did South Carolina secede, and when did Tennessee?

answer.where: The states in the Civil War, 1863 layer, legend and pop-ups. Union free state: 19. Union slave state (border state): 5 (Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, Missouri, West Virginia). Seceded before Fort Sumter: 7 (Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas). Seceded after Fort Sumter: 4 (Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia). South Carolina's pop-up: December 20, 1860. Tennessee's: June 8, 1861.
answer.accept: (a) 19, 5, 7 and 4. (b) Blue is the Union; orange is the Confederacy. (c) December 20, 1860 and June 8, 1861.
answer.text: South Carolina was the first to secede and Tennessee the last; students can confirm that by clicking the other orange states. The small northeastern states are easier to count after zooming in.

questions.task: Students predict where most battles were fought and write the prediction down before the battlefield layer goes on.
frontOfClass: Stay on The United States in 1863 bookmark with only the states layer on.
Ask: if you had to shade the part of this map where most of the fighting happened, where would you shade?
Have students write a prediction and a reason before anyone opens Map layers.

steps.en: Keep only The states in the Civil War, 1863 on.
Write your prediction before you turn on any other layer.

ask.en: Where on this map do you think most Civil War battles were fought: in the blue states, in the orange states, or along the line where they meet? Explain your thinking.

answer.accept: Any prediction with a reason drawn from the map, for example along the line between blue and orange because that is where the two sides met. Question 3 tests it; it is not marked right or wrong here.

questions.task: Students turn on the battlefield layer, test their prediction, and use pop-ups to find the few battlefields in Union free states.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Civil War battlefields.
Ask: was your prediction right? Which color has most of the dots?
Ask: which single state has the most?
Zoom to southern Pennsylvania and click the largest dark shape. Read the name, the state and the acres.
Ask: how many battlefields can you find in dark blue states?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Civil War battlefields.
Compare the dots on the blue states with the dots on the orange states.
Zoom in on Pennsylvania and click the largest battlefield. Read its pop-up.
Look for other battlefields in dark blue states.

ask.en: (a) Was your prediction right? Which color has most of the battlefields, and which state has the most of all? (b) What is the large battlefield in Pennsylvania, and about how many acres is it? (c) Are there many battlefields in the dark blue states, or few?

answer.where: Civil War battlefields layer over the states layer, and battlefield pop-ups. Most dots are on orange states, and Virginia has far more than any other state. Pennsylvania's large battlefield: Gettysburg, in Pennsylvania, about 73,600 acres. The dark blue (Union free) states have very few: two in Pennsylvania (Gettysburg and Hanover), two in Ohio, one in Indiana, four in Kansas and two in Minnesota.
answer.accept: (a) Orange, the states that seceded; Virginia. (b) Gettysburg, about 73,600 acres. (c) Few.
answer.text: Counted from the layer's state codes, not on the map: of 378 areas, 288 are in the eleven states that seceded (Virginia 121, Tennessee 38, Georgia 26; Louisiana's 23 include Yellow Bayou, whose code is mistyped L0), 62 are in the border states (Missouri 29, West Virginia 15, Kentucky 11, Maryland 7, Delaware none), 11 are in Union free states and 17 are outside the shaded states (15 named battlefields and the two unnamed areas).

questions.task: Students measure the distance between the two capitals, Washington, D.C. and Richmond, and use it to explain the crowd of battlefields in northern Virginia.
frontOfClass: Open the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark with the battlefields on.
Find Washington and Richmond. Washington was the capital of the United States; Richmond was the capital of the Confederacy.
Use Measure to draw a line from Washington to Richmond.
Ask: what do you notice about the battlefields near that line?
Click Maryland and Virginia and compare their groups.

steps.en: Open the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark.
Find Washington and Richmond. Each was the capital of one side.
Use Measure to find the distance between them in miles.
Click Maryland, then Virginia, and read the group in each pop-up.

ask.en: (a) About how far apart are Washington and Richmond? (b) What do you notice about the battlefields between and around them? (c) Maryland and Virginia both touch Washington. Which group is each in, and why would that matter to the United States government?

answer.where: Measure, from Washington to Richmond: about 95 to 100 miles in a straight line. Battlefields layer: a dense cluster between and around the two cities, including First Manassas and Second Manassas near Washington and several around Richmond and Petersburg. Maryland's pop-up: Union slave state (border state). Virginia's: Seceded after Fort Sumter (April 1861).
answer.accept: (a) About 100 miles. (b) They are crowded together between and around the two capitals. (c) Maryland stayed in the Union and Virginia seceded; if Maryland had also seceded, Washington would have been surrounded by Confederate states.
answer.text: Not on the map: Washington was the United States capital and Richmond was the Confederate capital from May 1861. Each army tried to threaten the other side's capital and protect its own, which is one reason so much fighting happened in the ground between them.

questions.task: Students turn on the railroads at the same bookmark, compare the networks north and south, and check whether battlefields sit on rail lines.
frontOfClass: Stay on the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark and turn on Railroads in operation by 1863.
Ask: where are the black railroad lines closest together, in the blue states or the orange states?
Find First Manassas, west of Washington, and Petersburg, south of Richmond.
Ask: what do those two battlefields have in common when the railroads are on?

steps.en: Stay on the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark.
In Map layers, turn on Railroads in operation by 1863.
Compare the railroads in Pennsylvania and Ohio with the railroads in Virginia and North Carolina.
Zoom in on the battlefields near Manassas and Petersburg and look at the railroads there.

ask.en: (a) Which side of this view has more railroads? (b) What do you notice about where the Manassas and Petersburg battlefields sit? (c) Why would an army fight for a place where railroads meet?

answer.where: Railroads in operation by 1863 layer with the battlefields on. Pennsylvania and Ohio are covered by a dense web of lines; Virginia and North Carolina have fewer, longer lines with wide gaps. The battlefields at Manassas and Petersburg both sit where railroad lines meet.
answer.accept: (a) The blue, Union side. (b) Both are at places where railroads cross or join. (c) Railroads carried soldiers, food and ammunition, so holding a junction helped one army and cut off the other.
answer.text: Summed from the layer, not on the map: about 23,000 miles of track in the Union states and about 9,000 miles in the states that seceded. The railroads only draw once the map is zoomed in to a region.

questions.task: Students move to the Mississippi Valley, find the string of battlefields along the river and work out what control of the river would do to the Confederacy.
frontOfClass: Open The Mississippi Valley bookmark with the battlefields on. Railroads can go off to make the river easier to see.
Trace the Mississippi River from Missouri down to the Gulf of Mexico.
Click three battlefields that touch the river and read their names.
Ask: which orange states are west of the river? What happens to them if the Union holds all of it?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn off Railroads in operation by 1863. Then open The Mississippi Valley bookmark.
Follow the Mississippi River south from Missouri to the Gulf of Mexico.
Click three battlefields on the river and write down their names.
Find the orange states that lie west of the river.

ask.en: (a) Name three battlefields on the Mississippi River. (b) Which states that seceded lie west of the river? (c) What would happen to those states if the Union controlled the whole river?

answer.where: Battlefields layer and pop-ups at The Mississippi Valley bookmark. On or beside the river, north to south: New Madrid Island No 10 (Missouri), Fort Pillow and Memphis (Tennessee), Helena (Arkansas), Vicksburg and Grand Gulf (Mississippi), Port Hudson, Baton Rouge and New Orleans (Louisiana). States layer: Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas are west of the river (part of Louisiana is east of it). Other areas on the river are also correct, for example Belmont (Missouri), Milliken's Bend, Goodrich's Landing, Donaldsonville and Forts Jackson & St. Philip (Louisiana). Memphis appears as Memphis I and Memphis II.
answer.accept: (a) Any three battlefields on the river, such as those named. (b) Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas. (c) They would be cut off from the rest of the Confederacy, and the Union could move troops and supplies along the river.
answer.text: Vicksburg's pop-up gives about 38,600 acres. The Battle of Vicksburg lesson picks up from here.

questions.task: Students find battlefields outside the shaded states and decide what the layer can and cannot tell them.
frontOfClass: Go back to The United States in 1863 bookmark with the battlefields on.
Ask: can you find dots that are not on any shaded state?
Click one and read the whole pop-up, including the last sentence.
Ask: what would you want to know about this battle that the pop-up does not say?

steps.en: Open The United States in 1863 bookmark with Civil War battlefields on.
Find a battlefield that is not on a shaded state. Zoom in until it is big enough to click, and click it.
Read the last sentence of the pop-up.

ask.en: (a) Where did you find a battlefield outside the shaded states? (b) What does the pop-up tell you about a battle, and what does it leave out? (c) Where could you look to find what is missing?

answer.where: Battlefields layer at the national view: dots in today's North Dakota, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Colorado and Idaho, none of them on a shaded state. Almost every battlefield pop-up gives the name, the state and the acres (two unnamed areas in Oklahoma do not), and each ends: "This layer does not say who won." The two exceptions are Sand Creek (Colorado) and Bear River (Idaho): their pop-ups say the area was an attack on a village, not a battle, so a student who clicks one of them has a different last sentence.
answer.accept: (a) Any of those places, for example North Dakota or New Mexico. (b) It gives the name, the state and the size of the area; it leaves out the date, who fought, who won and how many people were killed or wounded. (c) A National Park Service battle summary, a textbook, letters or newspapers from the time.
answer.text: Teacher notes say more about the western sites, which include fights between United States troops and Native nations and two massacres of Native people, at Bear River and Sand Creek.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from all three layers and at least one measurement or pop-up, then write one "why" question the map raised. Accept answers that say most battles were fought in the states that seceded and the border states, above all Virginia; that the ground between Washington and Richmond, railroad junctions and the Mississippi River drew the armies; and that few battles reached the Union free states.

student.en: Answer the big question, By 1863 the United States had split in two. Where was the Civil War fought, and why there?, using evidence from the states, the battlefields and the railroads. Finish with a question of your own that begins "Why": something about the war that the dots and lines made you wonder.

objectives: Sort the 35 states of 1863 into Union free states, border states and the states that seceded before and after Fort Sumter, using the legend and pop-ups.
Make and test a prediction about where Civil War battles were fought.
Measure the distance between Washington and Richmond and use it to explain the cluster of battlefields in Virginia.
Compare the railroad networks of the two sides and connect railroad junctions and the Mississippi River to where battles were fought.
Identify what the battlefield layer does not record and name a source that would.
discussion: Your prediction in question 2: what did you base it on, and how close was it?
Only a handful of battlefields are in dark blue states. What might that have meant for families living in Virginia compared with families living in Ohio?
The map shows where battles were fought but not who won. Does knowing where change how you think about the war?

differentiation.support: Questions 1 and 3 work well from the front with the legend open, and a printed list of nine of the river battlefields from the answer notes lets pairs check them off on the map in question 6.
differentiation.stretch: Use Measure to compare the length of the Mississippi from New Madrid to New Orleans with the distance from Washington to Richmond, and say what each number suggests about fighting in the West and in the East.

resources.title: Defining Battles of the Civil War

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the states layer (the four groups and which states border Washington), the battlefields layer (most dots on orange states, Virginia the most, Gettysburg as a rare battle in a free state), the Washington to Richmond measurement, the railroads (denser in the Union, junctions at Manassas and Petersburg) and the river battlefields.
assessment.exemplar: Most of the Civil War was fought in the South, and a lot of it in Virginia. When I turned on the battlefields, almost all the dots were on the orange states, and Virginia had the most by far. The dark blue states had only a few, like Gettysburg in Pennsylvania, which the pop-up says is about 73,600 acres. I think Virginia had so many because of the capitals. I measured from Washington to Richmond and it was only about 100 miles, and the battlefields are packed in between. The railroads matter too. The Union states have way more railroad lines, and Manassas and Petersburg are both where rail lines meet, so armies fought over them. In the Mississippi Valley the battlefields follow the river, like Vicksburg and Port Hudson. If the Union held the river, Texas, Arkansas and Louisiana were cut off. So the war was fought where the capitals, railroads and rivers were.

beforeYouStart.en: In 1860 and 1861, eleven states left the United States and formed the Confederate States of America. To secede means to leave a country. The states that stayed were called the Union. The attack on Fort Sumter, in South Carolina, in April 1861 started the fighting. This map shows the country in the middle of 1863.

readingTheMap.en: Blue states stayed in the Union: dark blue for free states, light blue for slave states that stayed (the border states). Orange states seceded: dark orange before Fort Sumter, light orange after. Only the states are on at the start; turn on the other layers in Map layers when a question asks. Dark shapes are battlefields; from far away each one looks like a dot. Thin black lines are railroads, and they appear only after you zoom in to a region. Each state's name is printed on it. Click a state or a battlefield to read its pop-up.

reflection.en: Which of the three layers changed your mind the most about where the war was fought, and what did it show you?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The map opens with only The states in the Civil War, 1863 on. Students turn on Civil War battlefields in question 3 and Railroads in operation by 1863 in question 5; the prediction in question 2 works best before either is on. Railroads draw only from the regional view inward, so they will not appear at The United States in 1863 bookmark. Battlefield pop-ups give the state as a two-letter code and do not give dates or results. Seventeen battlefield areas lie outside the shaded states: fifteen named battlefields in today's Oklahoma, North Dakota, New Mexico, Colorado, Idaho and Washington, D.C., and two unnamed areas in Oklahoma. In today's North Dakota, and at Fort Ridgely and Wood Lake in Minnesota, United States troops fought Sioux nations in the war years. Two of the sites were massacres of Native people by United States volunteer troops: Bear River, in today's Idaho, where a Northwestern Shoshone village was attacked in January 1863, and Sand Creek, in Colorado, where a Cheyenne and Arapaho village was attacked in November 1864. In Indian Territory (today's Oklahoma) Native nations fought on both sides of the Civil War, and the two New Mexico sites were battles between Union and Confederate troops. Question 7 asks students to find one of these dots; you may want to decide beforehand how much of that history to open up. West Virginia appears as its own state because it was admitted on June 20, 1863; its pop-up explains.

misconceptions.claim: All slave states joined the Confederacy.
misconceptions.response: The legend shows five slave states in light blue on the Union side: Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland and Missouri, which never seceded, and West Virginia, formed from Virginia's western counties in 1863.

misconceptions.claim: The war was fought evenly across the North and the South.
misconceptions.response: With the battlefields on, nearly all the dots are on the states that seceded and the border states; the Union free states have eleven.

misconceptions.claim: All eleven states seceded at once.
misconceptions.response: The two oranges show seven that seceded before Fort Sumter and four that seceded after; the pop-ups run from December 20, 1860 to June 8, 1861.

misconceptions.claim: A battlefield is a single spot.
misconceptions.response: Zoomed in, each battlefield is an area; Gettysburg's pop-up gives about 73,600 acres.

standards.text: Identify the division (Confederate and Union States, Border states, western territories) of the United States at the outbreak of the Civil War
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
